analysis.one_liner: Repeals five federal tax breaks for large oil and gas companies and adds a new tax on Gulf of Mexico drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on February 2, 2011 and never advanced, dying without a committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken away several federal tax deductions available to oil and gas companies with more than $100 million in annual revenue — including deductions for drilling costs and a special deduction for domestic production. It also would have created a new 13% tax on oil and gas drilled from federal waters in the Gulf of Mexico, with a credit for royalties companies already pay, and it would have limited a foreign tax credit that large oil companies use to lower their U.S. taxes. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiary would have been the federal treasury, since the bill raised revenue by closing deductions rather than creating a new program; to the extent that revenue offset other taxes or deficit spending, ordinary taxpayers would share the benefit. Gulf coast and public-land taxpayers would also have gained a more accurate accounting of the value of oil taken from federal waters. Small oil and gas producers were exempted from the deduction limits, so their competitive position relative to large companies would have improved.

how_it_helps.text: It denies five tax preferences — intangible drilling cost deductions, tertiary injectant deductions, the passive-loss exception, percentage depletion, and the domestic production deduction — to oil and gas companies with over $100 million in gross revenues, raising federal revenue from those companies.

It imposes a new 13% excise tax on oil and gas produced from federal leases in the Gulf of Mexico, with a credit for royalties already paid, so the public recoups more from drilling on federal waters.

It limits a foreign tax credit loophole that let large integrated oil companies count payments to foreign governments as taxes even when those payments bought specific economic benefits, closing a channel that reduced their U.S. tax bills.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil and gas companies with more than $100 million in gross revenue would have paid more in federal taxes through the loss of five deductions, the 7-year amortization requirement, and the foreign tax credit limits; Gulf of Mexico producers would have paid the new 13% excise tax. Some of those costs could have been passed to consumers through energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Opponents of repealing oil and gas tax preferences have argued that raising taxes on domestic producers can raise costs that show up in energy prices and reduce domestic drilling investment, an objection its supporters would have had to answer.

The bill would have imposed a new 13% excise tax on Gulf of Mexico production, which producers could pass through to refiners and ultimately consumers, and it preserved the same deductions for smaller companies, creating an uneven playing field between large and small producers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a straightforward tax increase on large oil and gas companies aimed at raising federal revenue; its costs were potentially higher prices or lower investment at the margins for consumers in oil-dependent regions, while small producers were explicitly carved out. Whether it was good policy turns on whether closing these deductions raises revenue efficiently or distorts drilling decisions — but the record here shows no debate on the merits: the Senate Finance Committee never considered it. The main cost of what actually happened is that a proposal supported by 12 senators was never tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 2011 by Senator Menendez with seven original cosponsors.
On the day of introduction it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action was taken: the Finance Committee held no vote, the Senate never debated it, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies are better off: every tax preference the bill would have denied them remained in place for the rest of the Congress, costing them nothing.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Close Big Oil Tax Loopholes Act on February 2, 2011.

for.name: 10 of 51 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Merkley, Whitehouse, Lautenberg, Reed, Boxer, Nelson of Florida, and Leahy as original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 2, 2011 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the 112th Congress.

against.name: American Petroleum Institute and the oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed repeal of oil and gas tax preferences during the 2011-2012 debate over oil company subsidies.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-held Senate.

industries.industry: Large oil and gas producers (over $100 million gross revenues)
industries.note: The bill would strip five major tax deductions, extend 7-year amortization of exploration costs, add a 13% excise tax on Gulf of Mexico production, and limit a foreign tax credit. Because the bill died in committee, these companies kept all of these preferences throughout the 112th Congress.

industries.industry: Small and independent oil and gas producers
industries.note: All the deduction restrictions applied only to taxpayers with gross revenues above $100 million, so smaller producers would have kept the deductions their larger competitors lost. They were effectively exempted from the bill.
Federal taxpayers would have gained revenue from the closed deductions and the new excise tax. The bill did not specify how that revenue would be used, so the benefit to the public was indirect.
